## Details

<a id="ia.robots-txt"></a>

### 1.1 robots.txt present

- Stable ID: `ia.robots-txt`
- Stage: Find
- Strength: MUST
- AR practices: AR-FIND-01 (mapping: full)
- Evidence type: `scanner_data`
- Fix: Serve a plain-text /robots.txt with at least one valid User-agent group.
- Fix workflow: [SKILL.md](../SKILL.md#ia.robots-txt)
- Evidence source: [agentready.org AR-FIND-01](https://www.agentready.org/#reachable)
- Pass condition: HTTP 200 text/plain document with at least one User-agent group
- Expected result: HTTP 200 with a text body that contains a User-agent line
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.robots-txt`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.robots-txt

Why: robots.txt is the universal standard for telling crawlers what they can access. AI crawlers like GPTBot, ClaudeBot and Googlebot-Extended check this file first before crawling your site.

References:

- [Google robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) (guide)
- [RFC 9309 - Robots Exclusion Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309) (spec)

Steps:

1. Create a file at the site root with the name robots.txt.
2. Add a User-agent group with Allow or Disallow rules that follow RFC 9309.

   ```text
   User-agent: *
   Allow: /

   Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml
   ```
3. Serve the file with HTTP 200 and the Content-Type text/plain.

Verify:

```bash
curl -sf https://{domain}/robots.txt
```

<a id="ia.ai-crawler-directives"></a>

### 1.2 AI crawler directives

- Stable ID: `ia.ai-crawler-directives`
- Stage: Find
- Strength: MUST
- AR practices: AR-FIND-01 (mapping: full)
- Evidence type: `scanner_data`
- Fix: Let the common AI user agents fetch your public pages in robots.txt.
- Fix workflow: [SKILL.md](../SKILL.md#ia.ai-crawler-directives)
- Evidence source: [agentready.org AR-FIND-01](https://www.agentready.org/#reachable)
- Expected result: No Disallow: / rule applies to GPTBot, ClaudeBot or the * group
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.ai-crawler-directives`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.ai-crawler-directives

Why: robots.txt determines which paths crawlers may fetch. This checkpoint measures effective crawl access for common AI user agents; it does not infer training consent.

References:

- [Google robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) (guide)
- [RFC 9309 - Robots Exclusion Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309) (spec)
- [OpenAI GPTBot documentation](https://platform.openai.com/docs/bots/gptbot) (guide)

Steps:

1. Find the rules in robots.txt that block AI user agents such as GPTBot, ClaudeBot and PerplexityBot.
2. Add an explicit Allow group for each AI user agent that may fetch your public pages.

   ```text
   User-agent: GPTBot
   Allow: /

   User-agent: ClaudeBot
   Allow: /

   User-agent: PerplexityBot
   Allow: /
   ```
3. Keep Disallow rules only for private paths, for example /account.

Verify:

```bash
curl -sf https://{domain}/robots.txt
```

### 1.3 XML sitemap

- Stable ID: `ia.xml-sitemap`
- Stage: Find
- Strength: SHOULD
- AR practices: AR-FIND-03 (mapping: full)
- Evidence type: `measured_study`
- Fix: Publish an XML sitemap and reference it in robots.txt.
- Fix workflow: [SKILL.md](../SKILL.md#ia.xml-sitemap)
- Evidence source: [agentready.org AR-FIND-03](https://www.agentready.org/#reachable)
- Pass condition: Valid XML sitemap that robots.txt references
- Expected result: HTTP 200 with an XML body that contains urlset or sitemapindex
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.xml-sitemap`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.xml-sitemap

Why: Sitemaps help AI crawlers discover all your pages efficiently. Without one, crawlers may miss important content or waste time discovering your site structure.

References:

- [Sitemaps XML protocol specification](https://www.sitemaps.org/protocol.html) (guide)
- [Google - Build and submit a sitemap](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/build-sitemap) (guide)

Steps:

1. Generate a sitemap.xml with a urlset or a sitemapindex root element.

   ```xml
   <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
   <urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
     <url><loc>https://example.com/</loc><lastmod>2026-10-01</lastmod></url>
   </urlset>
   ```
2. Add a Sitemap directive to robots.txt.

   ```text
   Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml
   ```

Verify:

```bash
curl -sf https://{domain}/sitemap.xml
```

### 1.4 llms.txt

- Stable ID: `ia.llms-txt`
- Stage: Read
- Strength: SHOULD
- AR practices: AR-READ-07 (mapping: full)
- Evidence type: `measured_study`
- Fix: Publish /llms.txt with an H1, a summary and Markdown links to your key pages on the canonical host.
- Fix workflow: [SKILL.md](../SKILL.md#ia.llms-txt)
- Evidence source: [agentready.org AR-READ-07](https://www.agentready.org/#read)
- Pass condition: Markdown file with an H1 and links to pages on the same host
- Expected result: HTTP 200 with a Markdown body that starts with an H1 and contains links
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.llms-txt`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.llms-txt

Why: llms.txt gives AI agents a curated entry point to your most important pages. Agents that fetch pages to complete a task get a short, structured overview instead of the full site.

References:

- [llms.txt specification](https://llmstxt.org/) (guide)
- [llms.txt proposal by Jeremy Howard](https://www.answer.ai/posts/2024-09-03-llmstxt.html) (guide)

Steps:

1. Create /llms.txt with an H1 title and a one-line blockquote summary.

   ```markdown
   # Example

   > Example sells project software for small teams.

   ## Docs

   - [Quick start](https://example.com/docs/start): set up an account
   - [API reference](https://example.com/docs/api): REST endpoints
   ```
2. Link only to pages on the canonical host that return HTTP 200.
3. Link /llms.txt from the home page or from a Link header so that agents find it.

Verify:

```bash
curl -sf https://{domain}/llms.txt
```

<a id="ia.meta-robots"></a>

### 1.5 Meta robots / X-Robots-Tag

- Stable ID: `ia.meta-robots`
- Stage: Find
- Strength: MUST
- AR practices: AR-FIND-01 (mapping: partial)
- Evidence type: `scanner_data`
- Fix: Remove restrictive robots directives from pages that agents must use.
- Fix workflow: [SKILL.md](../SKILL.md#ia.meta-robots)
- Evidence source: [agentready.org AR-FIND-01](https://www.agentready.org/#reachable)
- Expected result: No X-Robots-Tag header with noindex, noai or nosnippet
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.meta-robots`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.meta-robots

Why: Meta robots tags and X-Robots-Tag headers control per-page indexing. Restrictive directives like noindex or noai prevent AI systems from using your content.

References:

- [Google - Robots meta tag and X-Robots-Tag](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag) (guide)
- [MDN - Robots meta tag](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/meta/name#robots) (guide)

Steps:

1. Find noindex, nofollow, nosnippet, noai or noimageai in meta robots tags and in X-Robots-Tag headers.
2. Remove the directives from public pages, or set index and follow.

   ```html
   <meta name="robots" content="index, follow">
   ```

Verify:

```bash
curl -sI https://{domain}/
```

### 1.6 Content freshness signals

- Stable ID: `ia.content-freshness`
- Stage: Find
- Strength: MAY
- AR practices: none (mapping: none)
- Evidence type: `recommendation`
- Fix: Publish machine-readable publication and modification dates on editorial pages.
- Fix workflow: [SKILL.md](../SKILL.md#ia.content-freshness)
- Evidence source: [Schema.org dateModified property](https://schema.org/dateModified)
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.content-freshness`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.content-freshness

Why: Editorial pages can publish machine-readable modification and publication dates. This checkpoint validates those values only after the page is identified as editorial content.

References:

- [Schema.org dateModified property](https://schema.org/dateModified) (spec)
- [Open Graph article:modified_time](https://ogp.me/#type_article) (guide)

Steps:

1. Add datePublished and dateModified to the Article JSON-LD of each editorial page.

   ```json
   {
     "@context": "https://schema.org",
     "@type": "Article",
     "datePublished": "2026-09-01",
     "dateModified": "2026-10-01"
   }
   ```
2. Add the Open Graph tag article:modified_time with the same date.

   ```html
   <meta property="article:modified_time" content="2026-10-01T09:00:00Z">
   ```
3. Update dateModified only when the content changes.

Verify:

No read-only shell check exists. Use the rescan command.

<a id="ia.markdown-negotiation"></a>

### 1.7 Content negotiation (text/markdown)

- Stable ID: `ia.markdown-negotiation`
- Stage: Read
- Strength: MAY
- AR practices: AR-READ-09 (mapping: full)
- Evidence type: `measured_study`
- Fix: Return Markdown when a request sends Accept: text/markdown, and add Vary: Accept.
- Fix workflow: [SKILL.md](../SKILL.md#ia.markdown-negotiation)
- Evidence source: [agentready.org AR-READ-09](https://www.agentready.org/#read)
- Expected result: text/markdown
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.markdown-negotiation`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.markdown-negotiation

Why: AI agents fetch pages programmatically and benefit from machine-readable formats. Serving Markdown via Accept: text/markdown allows agents to consume structured content without HTML parsing overhead, saving up to 80% of tokens while preserving headings, links, and emphasis.

References:

- [HTTP Content Negotiation - MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Content_negotiation) (guide)
- [RFC 9110 - HTTP Semantics: Content Negotiation](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#name-content-negotiation) (spec)
- [Cloudflare: Introducing Markdown for Agents](https://blog.cloudflare.com/markdown-for-agents/) (guide)

Steps:

1. Generate a Markdown version of each content page.
2. Return the Markdown version with Content-Type text/markdown when the Accept header asks for it.
3. Add Vary: Accept so that caches keep the two formats apart.

   ```text
   Content-Type: text/markdown; charset=utf-8
   Vary: Accept
   ```

Verify:

```bash
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{content_type}\n' -H 'Accept: text/markdown' https://{domain}/
```

<a id="ia.bot-accessibility"></a>

### 1.8 HTTP bot accessibility

- Stable ID: `ia.bot-accessibility`
- Stage: Find
- Strength: MUST
- AR practices: AR-FIND-01 (mapping: full)
- Evidence type: `scanner_data`
- Fix: Return HTTP 200 to legitimate bots and do not block them in the WAF or CDN.
- Fix workflow: [SKILL.md](../SKILL.md#ia.bot-accessibility)
- Evidence source: [agentready.org AR-FIND-01](https://www.agentready.org/#reachable)
- Pass condition: HTTP 2xx for the home page
- Expected result: 200
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.bot-accessibility`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.bot-accessibility

Why: AI crawlers and agents must be able to fetch your pages via HTTP. If bots are blocked, AI systems cannot index or interact with your content.

References:

- [Cloudflare Bot Management documentation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/bots/) (guide)
- [Google crawlers and user agents overview](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/overview-google-crawlers) (guide)

Steps:

1. Request the home page with a bot user agent and record the HTTP status.
2. When the status is 401 or 403, add a WAF or CDN rule that allows known AI user agents.

   ```nginx
   map $http_user_agent $is_ai_bot {
     default       0;
     "~*GPTBot"    1;
     "~*ClaudeBot" 1;
   }
   ```
3. Keep rate limits, but do not answer verified AI crawlers with a challenge page.

Verify:

```bash
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -A 'GPTBot/1.0' https://{domain}/
```

### 1.9 Link response headers

- Stable ID: `ia.link-headers`
- Stage: Find
- Strength: MAY
- AR practices: AR-FIND-04, AR-READ-06 (mapping: partial)
- Evidence type: `recommendation`
- Fix: Advertise your API catalog, service description or documentation with an RFC 8288 Link header.
- Fix workflow: [SKILL.md](../SKILL.md#ia.link-headers)
- Evidence source: [agentready.org AR-FIND-04](https://www.agentready.org/#reachable)
- Expected result: A Link header with rel api-catalog, service-desc or service-doc
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.link-headers`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.link-headers

Why: RFC 8288 Link headers let an established API advertise concrete machine-readable descriptions and documentation. This checkpoint never creates its own API applicability.

References:

- [RFC 8288 - Web Linking](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8288) (spec)
- [IANA Link Relations registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/link-relations/link-relations.xhtml) (guide)
- [RFC 9727 - API Catalog (`api-catalog` link relation)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9727/) (spec)
- [RFC 9264 - Linkset media types](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9264) (spec)
- [OpenAPI Specification](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/latest.html) (spec)

Steps:

1. Add a Link header to the home page response that points to your API description.

   ```text
   Link: </.well-known/api-catalog>; rel="api-catalog", </openapi.json>; rel="service-desc"
   ```
2. Make sure that each linked resource returns HTTP 200.

Verify:

```bash
curl -sI https://{domain}/
```

<a id="ia.soft-404"></a>

### 1.13 Soft-404 hygiene

- Stable ID: `ia.soft-404`
- Stage: Read
- Strength: MUST
- AR practices: AR-READ-02 (mapping: full)
- Evidence type: `recommendation`
- Fix: Answer unknown paths with HTTP 404 or 410, not with HTTP 200 or a redirect.
- Fix workflow: [SKILL.md](../SKILL.md#ia.soft-404)
- Evidence source: [agentready.org AR-READ-02](https://www.agentready.org/#read)
- Pass condition: HTTP 404 or 410 for a path that does not exist
- Expected result: 404 or 410
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.soft-404`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.soft-404

Why: Agents and crawlers rely on a real 404 or 410 status to know a resource is missing. A 200 with the app shell (soft 404) makes them believe every probed path exists, pollutes indexes, and hides broken links from monitoring.

References:

- [Google Search Central: soft 404 errors](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/http-network-errors#soft-404-errors) (guide)
- [RFC 9110 section 15.5.5: 404 Not Found](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#name-404-not-found) (spec)

Steps:

1. Request a random path that does not exist and record the status.
2. Configure the server or the single-page app router to return 404 for unknown routes.

   ```nginx
   location / {
     try_files $uri $uri/ =404;
   }
   ```
3. Do not redirect unknown paths to the home page.

Verify:

```bash
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://{domain}/isagentready-missing-check
```

<a id="ia.dns-aid"></a>

### 1.14 DNS-AID agent records

- Stable ID: `ia.dns-aid`
- Stage: Find
- Strength: MAY
- AR practices: none (mapping: none)
- Evidence type: `recommendation`
- Fix: Publish an SVCB record for your agent index under _index._agents.
- Fix workflow: [SKILL.md](../SKILL.md#ia.dns-aid)
- Evidence source: [draft-mozleywilliams-dnsop-dnsaid: DNS for AI Discovery](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mozleywilliams-dnsop-dnsaid/)
- Expected result: exit code 0
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.dns-aid`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.dns-aid

Why: DNS-AID publishes agent discovery pointers under the _agents DNS names. This checkpoint detects SVCB or HTTPS answers and accepts an index TXT fallback; it does not verify the advertised service.

References:

- [draft-mozleywilliams-dnsop-dnsaid: DNS for AI Discovery](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mozleywilliams-dnsop-dnsaid/) (spec)
- [RFC 9460: SVCB and HTTPS resource records](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9460) (spec)

Steps:

1. Add an SVCB record at _index._agents.<zone> that points to your agent index.

   ```text
   _index._agents.example.com. 3600 IN SVCB 1 agents.example.com. alpn=h2
   ```
2. Add _mcp._agents and _a2a._agents records only for protocols that you serve.

Verify:

```bash
curl -sf -H 'accept: application/dns-json' 'https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?name=_index._agents.{domain}&type=SVCB' | jq -e '.Answer | length > 0'
```

## Informational checks

These training exposure checks do not change the score. They show how the site is exposed to AI training and bot verification.

| Legacy | Stable ID | Name | Stage | Strength | AR IDs | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| te.1 | [`ia.common-crawl-presence`](#ia.common-crawl-presence) | Common Crawl presence | Find | info | none | scanner_data |
| te.2 | [`ia.training-crawler-blocking`](#ia.training-crawler-blocking) | Training crawler blocking | Find | info | AR-FIND-01 | scanner_data |
| te.3 | [`ia.tdmrep`](#ia.tdmrep) | TDMRep declaration | Find | info | none | recommendation |
| te.4 | [`ia.ai-txt`](#ia.ai-txt) | ai.txt policy | Find | info | none | recommendation |
| te.5 | [`ia.web-bot-auth`](#ia.web-bot-auth) | Web Bot Auth | Find | info | none | recommendation |

<a id="ia.common-crawl-presence"></a>

### te.1 Common Crawl presence

- Stable ID: `ia.common-crawl-presence`
- Stage: Find
- Strength: informational (no strength)
- AR practices: none (mapping: none)
- Evidence type: `scanner_data`
- Fix: Decide if you want your content in public training archives, then set CCBot rules in robots.txt.
- Evidence source: [IsAgentReady benchmark](https://isagentready.com/en/research/state-of-agent-ready-web)
- Expected result: The latest index id. Query that index for url={domain} to see the presence.
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.common-crawl-presence`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.common-crawl-presence

Why: Common Crawl is a public web archive that many AI training sets use. This check reports if the domain is in the latest index. It is information only and does not change the score.

References:

- [Common Crawl](https://commoncrawl.org/) (guide)

Steps:

1. Decide if the content of the site may appear in public training archives.
2. To opt out, add a Disallow rule for CCBot to robots.txt.

   ```text
   User-agent: CCBot
   Disallow: /
   ```

Verify:

```bash
curl -sf 'https://index.commoncrawl.org/collinfo.json' | jq -r '.[0].id'
```

<a id="ia.training-crawler-blocking"></a>

### te.2 Training crawler blocking

- Stable ID: `ia.training-crawler-blocking`
- Stage: Find
- Strength: informational (no strength)
- AR practices: AR-FIND-01 (mapping: partial)
- Evidence type: `scanner_data`
- Fix: Set explicit rules for training crawlers that match your policy.
- Evidence source: [agentready.org AR-FIND-01](https://www.agentready.org/#reachable)
- Expected result: User-agent groups for the training crawlers that match your policy
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.training-crawler-blocking`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.training-crawler-blocking

Why: Some crawlers collect data for model training. This check reports which training crawlers robots.txt blocks. It is policy information and does not change the score.

References:

- [RFC 9309 - Robots Exclusion Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309) (spec)

Steps:

1. List the training crawlers that you want to allow or block, for example GPTBot, CCBot and Google-Extended.
2. Add a User-agent group for each crawler with Allow or Disallow.

   ```text
   User-agent: Google-Extended
   Disallow: /

   User-agent: GPTBot
   Allow: /
   ```
3. Keep search and user-triggered agents allowed, for example OAI-SearchBot and Claude-User.

Verify:

```bash
curl -sf https://{domain}/robots.txt
```

<a id="ia.tdmrep"></a>

### te.3 TDMRep declaration

- Stable ID: `ia.tdmrep`
- Stage: Find
- Strength: informational (no strength)
- AR practices: none (mapping: none)
- Evidence type: `recommendation`
- Fix: Publish /.well-known/tdmrep.json when you reserve text and data mining rights.
- Evidence source: [W3C TDM Reservation Protocol](https://www.w3.org/community/reports/tdmrep/CG-FINAL-tdmrep-20240202/)
- Expected result: exit code 0
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.tdmrep`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.tdmrep

Why: The W3C TDM Reservation Protocol lets a site reserve text and data mining rights in a machine-readable file. This check reports if the file exists. It does not change the score.

References:

- [W3C TDM Reservation Protocol](https://www.w3.org/community/reports/tdmrep/CG-FINAL-tdmrep-20240202/) (spec)

Steps:

1. Create /.well-known/tdmrep.json with one entry per path pattern.

   ```json
   [
     {"location": "/*", "tdm-reservation": 1, "tdm-policy": "https://example.com/tdm-policy.json"}
   ]
   ```
2. Serve the file as application/json with HTTP 200.

Verify:

```bash
curl -sf https://{domain}/.well-known/tdmrep.json | jq -e 'type == "array"'
```

<a id="ia.ai-txt"></a>

### te.4 ai.txt policy

- Stable ID: `ia.ai-txt`
- Stage: Find
- Strength: informational (no strength)
- AR practices: none (mapping: none)
- Evidence type: `recommendation`
- Fix: Publish /ai.txt only when you also keep robots.txt and Content-Usage rules aligned with it.
- Evidence source: [Spawning ai.txt](https://site.spawning.ai/spawning-ai-txt)
- Expected result: HTTP 200 with a plain-text policy
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.ai-txt`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.ai-txt

Why: ai.txt is an informal convention for a site policy on AI use. Few agents read it. This check reports if the file exists and does not change the score.

References:

- [Spawning ai.txt](https://site.spawning.ai/spawning-ai-txt) (guide)

Steps:

1. Write your AI use policy in /ai.txt as plain text.
2. Make sure that robots.txt and Content-Usage say the same.

Verify:

```bash
curl -sf https://{domain}/ai.txt
```

<a id="ia.web-bot-auth"></a>

### te.5 Web Bot Auth

- Stable ID: `ia.web-bot-auth`
- Stage: Find
- Strength: informational (no strength)
- AR practices: none (mapping: none)
- Evidence type: `recommendation`
- Fix: Publish /.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory when your site operates a signing bot.
- Evidence source: [HTTP Message Signatures directory draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-meunier-http-message-signatures-directory/)
- Expected result: exit code 0
- Rescan: `isagentready results {domain} --checkpoint ia.web-bot-auth`
- Details: https://isagentready.com/en/methodology/checkpoints/ia.web-bot-auth

Why: Web Bot Auth lets a bot sign its HTTP requests so that sites can verify it. A key directory at a well-known path publishes the public keys. This check reports if the directory exists.

References:

- [HTTP Message Signatures directory draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-meunier-http-message-signatures-directory/) (spec)

Steps:

1. Generate an Ed25519 key pair for your bot.
2. Publish the public key as a JWKS in the signatures directory.

   ```json
   {
     "keys": [{"kty": "OKP", "crv": "Ed25519", "x": "<base64url key>"}]
   }
   ```

Verify:

```bash
curl -sf https://{domain}/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory | jq -e '.keys | length > 0'
```
